claims.text: Current-dollar (nominal) PCE increased $23.7 billion (0.1 percent) from the preceding month in July 2022.

citations.quotation: Disposable personal income (DPI) increased $37.6 billion (0.2 percent) and personal consumption expenditures (PCE) increased $23.7 billion (0.1 percent).

claims.text: The nominal increase reflected a $33.3 billion increase in services spending, partly offset by a $9.6 billion decrease in goods spending.

citations.quotation: $23.7 billion increase in current-dollar PCE in July reflected an increase of $33.3 billion in spending for services that was partly offset by a decrease of $9.6 billion in spending for goods (table 3).

claims.text: The personal saving rate was 5.0 percent, with personal saving of $932.3 billion in July.

citations.quotation: Personal saving was $932.3 billion in July and the personal saving rate—personal saving as a percentage of disposable personal income—was 5.0 percent (table 1).

claims.text: Nominal (current-dollar) spending is distinct from the PCE price index: the price index decreased 0.1 percent in July, meaning the 0.1 percent nominal PCE increase occurred alongside slightly falling prices; real PCE rose 0.2 percent.

citations.quotation: The PCE price index decreased 0.1 percent. Excluding food and energy, the PCE price index increased 0.1 percent (table 9). Real DPI increased 0.3 percent in July and real PCE increased 0.2 percent; goods increased 0.2 percent and services increased 0.2 percent (tables 5 and 7).

claims.text: Current-dollar estimates are nominal, valued at prices of the period of the transaction; real values exclude price changes.

citations.quotation: Current-dollar estimates are valued in the prices of the period when the transactions occurred—that is, at “market value.” Also referred to as “nominal estimates” or as “current-price estimates.” Real values are inflation-adjusted estimates—that is, estimates that exclude the effects of price changes.

counterarguments.text: One might conflate the 0.1 percent PCE growth with the -0.1 percent price index change; the source explicitly separates the nominal spending increase from the price decrease, and real PCE rose 0.2 percent.
